clinicalPearls: TTH is recognized as bilateral, tight, band-like discomfort that builds gradually, fluctuates in intensity, and can persist near-continuously for days (Harrison 22e p.3514).

The most reliable bedside approach is to reserve the TTH label for headaches entirely lacking accompanying features such as nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia, throbbing quality, or worsening with movement (Harrison 22e p.3514).
Migraine is the principal differential of TTH; the presence of any migrainous accompaniment points away from TTH and toward migraine (Harrison 22e p.3514).

Patients who fit the TTH phenotype but also have migraine at other times, a family history of migraine, childhood migrainous syndromes, or typical migraine triggers may be biologically distinct from those with pure featureless TTH (Harrison 22e p.3514).

Diagnostic boundaries are genuinely blurred: the International Headache Society main definition permits some nausea, photophobia, or phonophobia, whereas the stricter appendix definition does not, and Harrison favors the appendix (feature-free) definition to separate TTH from migraine (Harrison 22e p.3514).

Among primary-care patients with headache lasting 3 months or more and no neurologic symptoms or signs, fewer than 10% actually have TTH and more than 90% have migraine, so a confident TTH label in this setting is uncommon (Harrison 22e p.3514).
TTH is the most prevalent primary headache type overall, accounting for roughly 69% of primary headaches in a population series (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-1).
harrison.pathophysiology: The mechanism of TTH is incompletely understood. Harrison favors a primary disorder of central nervous system pain modulation alone, contrasting it with migraine, which involves more generalized disturbance of sensory modulation. Despite the name, there is no clear evidence that nervous tension is causative; importantly, muscle contraction does NOT reliably distinguish TTH from migraine, as no difference in contraction is seen between the two headache types. A genetic contribution has been suggested but is unreliable, since current diagnostic criteria likely contaminated those studies with migraine patients (Harrison 22e p.3514).
additionalDifferentials: Migraine (the main differential, defined by migrainous accompaniments TTH lacks) (Harrison 22e p.3514)
Migraine-TTH overlap / mixed phenotype with intercurrent migraine attacks (Harrison 22e p.3514)
nonInfectiousMimics: Chronic migraine within the chronic daily headache spectrum (Harrison 22e p.158, Table 17-3)
Medication-overuse headache (refractory daily/near-daily headache from analgesic overuse) (Harrison 22e p.158-159)
Other secondary causes of chronic daily headache: post-traumatic, inflammatory (e.g., giant cell arteritis, sarcoidosis, Behcet syndrome), and chronic CNS infection (Harrison 22e p.158, Table 17-3)
additionalInvestigations: TTH is a clinical diagnosis; neuroimaging is not routine but CT or MRI of the brain is indicated when the examination is abnormal or the headache is recent-onset, with CT and MRI being comparably sensitive as initial screens (Harrison 22e p.157).
Lumbar puncture may be required when a serious secondary cause is suspected and a benign etiology cannot otherwise be established (Harrison 22e p.157).

General evaluation of acute headache may add palpation of cranial arteries, cervical spine assessment, blood pressure and urine for cardiovascular/renal status, and ocular examination including funduscopy and intraocular pressure (Harrison 22e p.157).
redFlags: Sudden-onset or first severe headache, or the 'worst headache ever' (Harrison 22e p.156-157, Table 17-2)
Vomiting preceding the headache (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2)
Subacute worsening over days or weeks (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2)
Pain provoked by bending, lifting, or coughing (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2)
Pain that disturbs sleep or is present immediately on awakening (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2)
Fever or unexplained systemic signs, or a known systemic illness (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2)
Local tenderness, e.g., over the temporal artery region (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2)
Serious secondary causes to consider with new severe headache include meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, epidural/subdural hematoma, glaucoma, tumor, and purulent sinusitis (Harrison 22e p.157)
harrison.prognosis: TTH is classified as episodic when infrequent and chronic when occurring on 15 or more days per month; the pain fluctuates and may persist near-continuously for many days. Chronic TTH falls within the chronic daily headache group, which carries considerable disability, and may be complicated by medication overuse (Harrison 22e p.3514, p.158).
pitfalls: Over-applying the TTH label: in chronic headache without neurologic signs, more than 90% of patients actually have migraine, so TTH is frequently overdiagnosed (Harrison 22e p.3514).
Assuming muscle contraction confirms TTH; it does NOT distinguish TTH from migraine (Harrison 22e p.3514).
Overlooking medication overuse, which can convert episodic headache into refractory daily/near-daily headache and blunt the effect of preventive treatment (Harrison 22e p.158-159).
Mistaking a serious secondary headache for benign primary headache when an underlying cause has activated or worsened the primary syndrome (Harrison 22e p.158).
harrison.severityClassification: Pain is characteristically mild to moderate, bilateral, tight and band-like, and non-throbbing. By frequency the IHS scheme distinguishes infrequent episodic, frequent episodic, chronic (>=15 days/month), and probable TTH; Harrison emphasizes the episodic-versus-chronic distinction (Harrison 22e p.3514, p.155 IHS classification).
